prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Willie had a stubborn wart upon his middle toe. Regardless, though, of what he tried the wart refused to go. So Willie went and visited his family foot physician, who instantly agreed it was a stubborn wart condition. The doctor tried to squeeze the wart. He tried to twist and turn it. He tried to scrape and shave the wart. He tried to boil and burn it. He poked it with a pair of tongs. He pulled it with his tweezers. He held it under heat lamps, and he crammed it into freezers. Regrettably these treatments were of very little use. He looked at it and sputtered, “Ach! I cannot get it loose!” “I’ll have to get some bigger tools to help me to dissect it. I’ll need to pound and pummel it, bombard it and inject it.” He whacked it with a hammer, and he yanked it with a wrench. He seared it with a welding torch despite the nasty stench. He drilled it with a power drill. He wrestled it with pliers. He zapped it with a million volts from large electric wires. He blasted it with gamma rays, besieged it with corrosives, assaulted it with dynamite and nuclear explosives. He hit the wart with everything, but when the smoke had cleared, poor Willie’s stubborn wart remained, and Willie’d disappeared.

Willie had a very persistent wart growing on the middle toe of his foot. No matter what remedy he attempted, it simply would not leave. Eventually, he went to see the foot doctor his family used, and the physician immediately confirmed that the wart was an especially obstinate one.

The doctor first attempted to press it. Then he twisted it and turned it. He scraped at it, shaved it down, heated it, and tried to burn it away. He jabbed it with tongs, tugged at it with tweezers, placed it beneath warming lamps, and even subjected it to freezing cold.

Unfortunately, none of these methods helped much. Staring at the wart, the doctor muttered, “Ach! I can’t remove this thing!” He decided he would need much larger equipment to cut it apart, saying he would have to strike it, batter it, attack it, and inject it.

So he smashed it with a hammer and pulled at it using a wrench. He scorched it with a welding torch, even though it produced a terrible smell. He bored into it with an electric drill, grappled with it using pliers, and shocked it with a million volts from huge electrical cables.

He bombarded it with gamma radiation, surrounded it with caustic chemicals, and attacked it with dynamite as well as nuclear explosives. The doctor used every possible weapon against the wart, but when the smoke finally lifted, Willie’s stubborn wart was still there—and poor Willie was gone.
outputs.L3:
Willie had a stubborn wart on the middle toe of his left foot, and no matter what he did, it refused to go away. He soaked it, wrapped it, rubbed it with ointments, covered it with bandages, and waited patiently for it to shrink. But the wart remained exactly where it was, as firm and unpleasant as ever.

At last, Willie went to see the family foot physician. The doctor examined the wart carefully, peering at it from every angle and pressing it with a thoughtful frown. After a long silence, he nodded gravely and admitted that Willie was dealing with an unusually stubborn wart.

The doctor began with the usual treatments. He squeezed the wart, scraped it, burned it, froze it, and even tried pulling it. Each time, Willie winced and hoped the problem was finally solved. But each time, when the smoke cleared or the ice melted, the wart was still there, unchanged and unimpressed.

Since ordinary methods had failed, the doctor became more determined. He brought out stronger and stranger tools. He tried drills, electric currents, radiation, harsh corrosive chemicals, and, eventually, methods that seemed much too dramatic for a single toe. Still, nothing worked. The wart resisted every attempt.

By the end of the doctor’s exhausting campaign, the examination room was a wreck. The instruments were bent, the floor was scorched, and the air smelled faintly of smoke and chemicals. Yet the wart remained intact.

Willie, however, had disappeared.
outputs.L4:
Willie had a wart on the end of his toe.

It was not a grand wart, nor even a very large one, but it was a stubborn wart. It sat there calmly, round and firm, as if it owned the toe and had signed a long lease. Willie tried to ignore it at first. He wore thicker socks. He walked on the other side of his foot. He even told himself that a wart was not worth worrying about.

But the wart remained.

At last Willie went to see a foot doctor, a serious man with shining instruments, polished spectacles, and the confident air of someone who believed no wart could stand against modern science.

“Ah,” said the doctor, peering at Willie’s toe. “A simple case.”

He took out a tiny knife, a bottle of medicine, and a roll of bandage. He scraped, dabbed, wrapped, and nodded.

“There,” he said. “That should do it.”

But it did not do it.

The next week Willie returned. The bandage came off, and there was the wart, looking just as comfortable as before.

“Hmm,” said the doctor. “More resistant than I expected.”

This time he used a sharper instrument, a stronger medicine, and a longer bandage. He clipped and pared and painted the toe with something that smelled like lightning trapped in a bottle.

“That will certainly finish it,” he declared.

But it did not finish it.

The wart stayed.

After that the doctor became determined. No ordinary wart was going to embarrass him. He brought out files, clamps, drills, needles, and curious little machines that hummed and clicked. He scraped the wart. He burned the wart. He froze the wart. He shocked it with electricity until Willie’s hair stood straight up and the lamps in the office flickered.

The wart remained.

The doctor frowned.

“This is no common wart,” he said. “We must take stronger measures.”

Willie, who had begun to feel less enthusiastic about the whole business, asked whether perhaps the wart might simply be left alone.

“Left alone?” cried the doctor. “Never! That would be surrender.”

So the treatments grew more extreme.

The doctor soaked Willie’s toe in acids, powders, oils, and ointments of terrifying colors. He wrapped it in steaming poultices. He applied magnets, batteries, springs, and suction cups. He used a little saw, a little pump, and once, for reasons Willie never understood, a small brass horn.

Still the wart sat there.

By now the doctor was no longer calm. He studied thick medical books late into the night. He sent away for special equipment. He consulted charts, diagrams, and mysterious formulas. When Willie came back again, the office had changed. The comfortable chair was gone, replaced by straps, tubes, wires, and a machine with a red switch marked “CAUTION.”

“Doctor,” said Willie nervously, “are you quite sure this is necessary?”

“Necessary?” said the doctor. “My dear boy, it is scientific.”

He pressed the switch.

There was a buzz, a flash, a bang, and a smell like burned toast. Smoke filled the room. When it cleared, the doctor inspected Willie’s toe.

The wart was still there.

The doctor’s face went pale. Then it turned red. Then it became the face of a man who had stopped treating a wart and had begun fighting a war.

“Very well,” he said. “If science is not enough, we shall use engineering.”

The next appointment took place not in the office but in a shed behind it. There were pulleys, hammers, tanks, hoses, coils of wire, and a machine that looked as though it had once belonged to a railway company. Willie’s toe was placed carefully beneath a complicated arrangement of levers.

“This device,” said the doctor proudly, “will remove the wart with perfect accuracy.”

He pulled the lever.

The machine groaned. The floor shook. A wheel spun loose and rolled through the wall. Somewhere a whistle blew.

The wart remained.

The doctor wiped soot from his spectacles.

“One final treatment,” he said.

Willie should have gone home then. He should have put on his shoe, thanked the doctor politely, and decided to live a long and peaceful life with the wart. But the doctor spoke with such solemn confidence, and Willie had already come so far, that he allowed himself to be led to a field outside town.

In the middle of the field stood a small mound of earth. Wires ran from the mound to a box behind a stone wall.

“What is that?” asked Willie.

“A carefully controlled explosive charge,” said the doctor. “Just enough to remove the wart. Nothing more.”

“Nothing more?” said Willie.

“Nothing more,” said the doctor.

Willie placed his foot exactly where the doctor pointed. The doctor retreated behind the wall and counted.

“Three. Two. One.”

There was a tremendous explosion.

Birds flew from the trees. Windows rattled for miles around. A cloud of dust rose into the sky and drifted slowly away.

When the doctor finally came out from behind the wall, he looked around.

There was a hole in the field.

There were Willie’s shoes, or parts of them.

There was no Willie.

And on the edge of the crater, sitting on a small piece of toe-shaped bandage, was the wart.

It looked entirely unharmed.

The doctor stared at it for a long time. Then he closed his medical bag, cleared his throat, and walked away without saying a word.

And that is why, whenever anyone proposes a very large solution to a very small problem, people who know the story of Willie and his wart tend to step back, cover their toes, and suggest trying something simpler first.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny, darkly comic rhyming poem in the style of Shel Silverstein about a boy named Willie who has an indestructible wart on his toe, with increasingly absurd treatments that end with Willie disappearing but the wart remaining.
counterfactuals.output:
There once was a boy with a wart on his toe,  
A terrible, terrible wart named Joe.  
It wrinkled and winked and itched in the night,  
And glowed in the dark with a fungus-green light.

His mother said, “Willie, that bump has to go!”  
But the wart said, “Ha!” and continued to grow.  
They scrubbed it with soap till the bathtub turned black—  
The wart just grew eyebrows and started to quack.

They soaked it in vinegar, pickle juice, glue,  
And grandmother’s soup from nineteen-forty-two.  
They wrapped it in bacon and tied it with string—  
The wart ate the bacon and burped like a king.

A doctor arrived with a saw and a grin,  
Said, “This may hurt lots, but we’ll try not to win.”  
He snipped and he clipped with a shiny steel snort—  
The scissors broke off and were filed in court.

They called in a wizard with thunder and smoke,  
Who chanted a chant and then vanished—poor bloke.  
His hat fluttered down with a note tied in lace:  
“Your wart is too strong. I am leaving this place.”

They froze it with ice from the dark side of Mars,  
They zapped it with lasers and bottled-up stars.  
They fed it a potion that dragons all dread—  
The wart grew a mouth and politely said, “Bread?”

So Willie got tired, as tired boys do,  
Of one stubborn wart and one stubborn shoe.  
He packed up his socks and he packed up his cat,  
And said, “If it stays, then I’m done with all that.”

They launched him by cannon clean over the moon,  
With a lunch and a note that said, “Please come back soon.”  
There came a small *poof* and a faraway cry—  
Then silence dripped down from the marmalade sky.

Now Willie is gone, not a freckle, not hair,  
Not a sneeze, not a shoe, not a whisper of air.  
But there on the doorstep, all wrinkled and slow,  
Sits Joe, the old wart, with ten toes in a row.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a children’s nonsense poem about a stubborn wart that doctors try to remove using ridiculous tools and over-the-top methods, escalating from tweezers and heat lamps to dynamite and nuclear explosions.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wart That Wouldn’t Go**

There once was a wart on Wilhelmina’s knee,  
As round as a pea and as proud as could be.  
It winked at the doctors and shouted, “No way!  
I’m planning to sit here forever and stay!”

They pinched it with tweezers of silvery steel,  
But the wart only giggled, “That gives me a tickle!”  
They shone it with heat lamps, all glowing and bright,  
It put on sunglasses and basked in the light.

They scrubbed it with soap from a whale-shaped spoon,  
They sang it a lullaby slightly off-tune.  
They bonked it with pillows, they blew it a kiss,  
The wart gave a yawn and said, “Doctors, you miss!”

They brought in a plunger, a trumpet, a rake,  
A waffle-iron warmer, a birthday cake.  
They tickled its corners with feathers and glue,  
The wart painted freckles and shouted, “Yahoo!”

“Enough!” cried the doctors. “We’ll try something bigger!”  
They built a huge gadget with springs and a trigger.  
It whirred and it clanged and it puffed purple smoke—  
The wart merely coughed and said, “Is this a joke?”

They rolled in a cannon that fired marshmallow,  
A blizzard of custard, a geyser of Jell-O.  
The room became sticky from ceiling to floor,  
But the wart only asked, “Have you doctors got more?”

So out came the dynamite, fizzy and red—  
“Stand back!” all the nurses and noodle-cooks said.  
KABLOOIE! went confetti, with whistles and sparks—  
The wart wore a party hat covered in stars.

At last, very desperate, wrinkled, and pale,  
They ordered a rocket as big as a whale.  
“A nuclear BOOM!” cried the chief with a frown.  
“We’ll blast that old wart to the next silly town!”

The rocket went WHOOSH to the moon and came back,  
The sky turned to licorice, purple, and black.  
The BOOM was so giant it rattled the sun—  
And everyone sneezed when the echo was done.

When smoke cleared away from the hospital chart,  
There sat Wilhelmina… and there sat the wart.  
It polished its bump and declared with a grin,  
“I’m terribly stubborn. I simply won’t thin!”

Then Wilhelmina said, “Wart, let’s be friends.  
I’m tired of booms and explosive loose ends.”  
The wart blushed politely and whispered, “All right,”  
Then packed up its suitcase and left in the night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create a humorous rhyming story-poem where a kid visits a foot doctor for a wart, and the doctor keeps trying more extreme procedures until the joke ending is that the wart survives but the kid does not?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wart That Wouldn’t Part**

Young Milo had a wart one day,  
A bump upon his toe,  
It winked at him each morning-time  
And whispered, “I won’t go.”

His mother said, “A foot doctor  
Will fix that little dot.”  
The wart put on a tiny hat  
And said, “I’d rather not.”

The doctor peered through giant specs  
And gave a learned report:  
“A classic stubborn wart,” he said,  
“The most annoying sort.”

He dabbed it with a potion first,  
All fizzy, green, and tart.  
The wart just burped politely and  
Refused again to part.

He froze it with a frosty spray  
That made the curtains snow.  
The wart put on a knitted scarf  
And murmured, “Pip-pip, no.”

He zapped it with a laser beam  
That hummed a disco tune.  
The wart began to boogie and  
Lit up the whole exam room.

He strapped on gloves, he rang a bell,  
He wheeled in “Plan Thirteen”:  
A chrome-and-copper Wart-O-Matic,  
Dreadful, loud, and mean.

It clanked, it clunked, it launched a puff  
Of smoke and purple sparks.  
The wart said, “Lovely ambiance!  
But still, I’m leaving marks.”

The doctor frowned. “This calls for more.  
Bring forth the heavy gear!”  
A tiny marching band came in  
And played beside Milo’s ear.

He tried a drill, a chant, a fan,  
A cream made out of cheese,  
A trained raccoon, a cannonball,  
And seven angry bees.

At last he sighed, “One final chance!”  
His voice was grim and grave.  
He pressed a button labeled:  
**DO NOT PRESS — BEHAVE.**

There came a flash, a thunderclap,  
A smell of burnt shampoo.  
The room was gone, the chair was gone,  
The doctor’s left shoe too.

And on the floor, amid the smoke,  
Still perched upon that toe,  
The wart tipped up its tiny hat  
And said, “I told you so.”

The doctor lived. The wart lived on,  
Defiant, round, and squat.  
As for poor Milo? Let’s just say…  
He very much did not.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a macabre silly poem with an AABB rhyme scheme about Willie’s wart on his middle toe that won’t go away, including lots of verbs like scrape, burn, drill, zap, blast, and ending with the wart still there.
counterfactuals.output:
Willie had a wart on his middle toe,  
A knobbly blob with a ghastly glow.  
He’d scrape it nightly with a spoon,  
And burn it blue beneath the moon.  

He tried to drill it, zap it, blast,  
He hollered, “Surely now it’s passed!”  
He picked and poked with wicked glee,  
Then boiled it briefly in his tea.  

He stomped it flat with coffin shoes,  
Then rubbed it down with graveyard ooze.  
He froze it, fried it, filed it bare,  
And chased it round with dragon air.  

The wart just winked and gave a grin,  
Then sprouted one small whiskery chin.  
Poor Willie shrieked, “It isn’t fair!”  
But on his toe—the wart’s still there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a whimsical but morbid poem for children about an impossible-to-remove toe wart, using exaggerated medical slapstick and a final twist where Willie disappears in the smoke.
counterfactuals.output:
**Willie’s Wonderful Worrisome Wart**

Young Willie had a wart one day  
Upon his little toe,  
It winked at him at breakfast-time  
And seemed to hum “Hello!”

His mother cried, “Oh, mercy me!”  
His father dropped his spoon.  
The doctor came with seventeen  
Big bandages and a balloon.

They scrubbed it with a toothbrush,  
They tickled it with string,  
They wrapped it up in mustard paste  
And taught the cat to sing.

The nurse arrived with rubber gloves,  
A trumpet, and a mop.  
She shouted, “Stand back, everyone!  
This wart is fit to pop!”

They froze it with an ice-cream truck,  
They warmed it with a lamp,  
They stamped a little “CANCELLED” sign  
Upon its bumpy camp.

They tried a tiny cannonball,  
A magnet, glue, and tea,  
A plunger and a pirate’s hook—  
But still it would not flee.

The surgeon brought a silver saw  
As shiny as the moon.  
“It’s only for dramatic flair,”  
He said, “I’ll use a spoon.”

He scooped and spun and slipped and slid,  
Then landed in the sink.  
The wart just yawned a wartish yawn  
And turned a deeper pink.

At last they mixed a fizzy brew  
Of soap and sneeze and lime,  
With powdered socks and cough-drop rocks  
And one loud nursery rhyme.

It bubbled green, it bubbled blue,  
It burped a cloud of red—  
“Good gracious!” whispered Willie,  
As smoke rose round his bed.

The wart was gone! The toe was bare!  
They cheered from floor to ceiling—  
But when the smoke had cleared away,  
Poor Willie was gone too, concealing.

They searched the socks, they searched the shoes,  
They searched beneath the stair—  
And sometimes, when the bathtub steams,  
You’ll hear him giggle there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
